The CP2K program package, often seen as an indispensable tool for chemistry and physics research, has just released its latest version, 8.3, which boasts impressive speed, especially when leveraging modern architectures like GPU accelerators. This new release adds robust support for quantum materials, thanks to a comprehensive library for periodic systems, while its linear system solver now benefits from parallel communication over GPUs. Additionally, the new release includes a range of utility programs that facilitate the creation of an adaptive sparse grid, a high-performance random number generator, and more. This version also includes numerous bug fixes and optimizations, further solidifying CP2K's status as one of the fastest atomic-scale ab initio simulation codes available. With its recent "short" version, 8.3u2, and a range of other updates, CP2K is well-positioned to take advantage of the growing capabilities offered by high-performance computing facilities and hardware, all while remaining accessible to researchers and developers.

Small high-energy flares observed in the solar corona have been notoriously difficult to detect. Despite improvements in sensitivity, the smallest solar X-ray flares have evaded detection for decades. A study claims to have successfully detected these tiny whispy structures in the solar corona using the FOXSI (Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager) instrument. FOXSI is a space-based telescope that uses a reflective mirror to focus X-rays and observe the solar corona in the 5-10 keV energy range. Observations of multiple solar events confirm the presence of faint emission, with measurable counts rising above background levels and providing a clear signal-to-noise ratio. The instrument's sensitivity is so advanced that it can detect these tiny whispy structures with lower flare intensities, in line with previous predictions.

In our daily lives, forecasts influenced by social elements, such as human interactions and media presence, are common. For instance, during a viral event, predictions for items like hoodies and face masks rapidly rise. To reflect changing social trends, our approach involves integrating the duration of training and testing into the forecasting model. The implementation of our method is demonstrated on the dataset of social media-driven sales data, where the inclusion of test-driven duration information leads to a 2.5% absolute gain in predictive accuracy compared to conventional techniques.

A newly developed Recurrent Equation System, derived from Euler-Arnold equations, is providing valuable insights into the underlying structure of Conformal Field Theory. By employing a specially designed solution decomposition approach, researchers are now able to achieve notable advancements in both solution computation and Casimir field generation, even in cases with existing Liouville field limitations. This breakthrough also offers potential avenues for developing a non-singular, conformal invariant path integral formulation in four dimensions. Furthermore, the newly developed framework is exhibiting remarkable applicability, with successful translation to a variety of more complex frameworks such as N=1 super conformal field theories and a novel, novel gauge invariant way of performing a null surface canonical reduction.

A method for determining the optimal position of a platform in a factor graph is described. This is achieved by minimizing the variance of the measurements, and it can be effectively carry out a full least squares optimization. However, achieving closure for the covariance of the nonlinear equations proves to be a difficult task, and therefore an approximate solution is developed using a successive linearization approach. When the approximate covariance is sufficient, the problem can be solved directly using an efficient and fast algorithm. This efficient approach allows for the removal of unnecessary factors, reducing the complexity of the problem and potentially allowing for a closed form solution. This ideal configuration is presented as a method for solving a specific problem, and future research will explore the extension of this framework to more complex scenarios.

The concept of eternal inflation suggests that our universe could be one tiny fragment of an infinitely complex cosmic landscape, with an unpredictably vast number of separate "sectors" emerging from different vacuum states. These "concealed" sectors, characterized by unique physical properties, may exist within this vast landscape, (possibly) including a thermally fluctuating "hidden" universe with multiple degrees of freedom. With an incredibly high number of states, the likelihood of this "hidden" universe also possessing multiple degrees of freedom and being driven by an imbalance in energy and entropy grows exponentially. This "hidden" universe may give rise to a variety of phenomena, such as the appearance of baryonatic particles and a radiation-dominated cosmology, potentially giving rise to a multiverse composed of a thermally fluctuating "hidden" universe and our "visible" universe, each with distinct properties and a shared origin.

Searches for same-sign W boson pairs in the jets and high-pT same-sign muons or electrons final states have been conducted using the CMS detector at the LHC. Proton-proton collisions took place at a 13 TeV energy at the CMS experiment, accumulating 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of data that corresponds to an inverse luminosity of  5.78 x 10$^{34}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-2}$. No signal was found for unusual occurrences beyond those predicted by the standard model, establishing new standards at the 55.2 fb$^{-2}$ level for same-sign W boson pair events, with masses under 3 TeV for the combined results. A study of same-sign W boson pair production in the CMS experiment provides the strongest restrictions until now on electroweak production of this phenomenon at 6.6 fb$^{-2}$, together with a comparison with analogous findings of same-sign top quark pairs, and same-sign Z boson pairs in electroweak processes.

In the field of computer vision, camera adjustment, particularly lens tinting, is critical for capturing clear images of subjects in bright light, preventing overexposure that can distort data. A novel, universal method for tinted camera capture is presented here, enabling the use of any camera without requiring calibration. By incorporating a single universal filter, our approach effectively controls exposure across multiple devices, achieving reliable results on various capture systems, as demonstrated by our data and evaluations.

The evidence for a particular type of universe expansion, as well as the shape of space itself, has been extensively examined using a variety of techniques, including the analysis of galaxy distributions and the way the universe's expansion affects the phenomenon known as the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation. Our study applies a technique for measuring the universe's 3D structure, called the Reduced Offset Method, to investigate the consistency of spatial distributions from the Planck satellite's data with a particular type of universe model. A test of this consistency shows a high level of favor towards a universe model with a particular type of curvature, as well as a particular rate of expansion. While these findings are close to the values predicted by a previous model, known as the $\Lambda$CDM, our analysis reveals a noticeable disparity, particularly in terms of a measure of how quickly the universe's expansion is changing. A further observation reveals that a particular type of universe model with a particular type of curvature, as well as a particular rate of expansion, can better explain a set of observations related to a phenomenon known as the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation. Our findings are consistent with a previous finding, as well as a previous model's prediction, when taking into account a particular type of uncertainty. A particular type of universe model with a particular type of curvature, as well as a particular rate of expansion, is shown to be a reasonable fit for a combination of a particular type of curvature's effect and a phenomenon known as the B

Software maintenance is a labor-intensive, costly process, with a large portion devoted to rectifying defects found in the existing code base. Despite the abundance of data available from popular version control systems like GitHub, maintaining quality standards proves difficult, particularly when tackling the fragmented nature of maintenance tasks. To address this challenge, we propose the concept of meta-maintenance, which involves identifying useful activities within the developers' daily routines, extracting these activities across diverse projects, and applying this knowledge to improve maintenance efficiency. By analyzing a year's worth of data from GitHub, we demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of meta-maintenance, showcasing its potential to expand the scope of maintenance efficiency from individual projects to the entire software ecosystem.

The 2008 and 2009 observations of the eclipsing binary system BD And revealed valuable insights into its nature. Calculations yielded a mass ratio of 0.97 and photometric data provided further clarity on the detached system's characteristics. Data indicated a minimal temperature difference of approximately 40 K between its components, fulfilling the requirements of a gamma Doradus variable. Nevertheless, due to limited data availability, its periodicity remains uncertain. BD And's 2.859 day orbital cycle and short precession period for its non-uniform rotation make it a peculiar system with both similar and distinct characteristics to well-known SB binaries.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved developing a Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrated the existence of a self-similar solution. The current research expands on that study by altering the initial data's growth rate in a local $L^p$ space (with $p > 100$) and showing that under these conditions, the modified Yamabe flow converges to a Gaussian. Specifically, it includes two key scenarios - one where the initial data decays at a faster rate and another where it decays at a slower rate. The more favorable scenario of slower decay includes data from all $L^p$ spaces ($p > 100$), whereas the more stringent requirements of being square-integrable and having second-order integrable curvature are necessary for the less favorable scenario of faster decay. The implementation of a dynamic renormalization group via backward time translation is what allows the less favorable scenario of faster decay to be included in the analysis.

Existing cooperative recommendation methods focus on learning the preference of users for overall product attributes, neglecting the uniqueness of attribute patterns across different domains. As a result, their performance is suboptimal in multi-sparse-domain scenarios. To address this limitation, a new method called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) is proposed. MSDCR uses a multi-task framework that enables coordinated preference learning across multiple domains, leveraging the shared patterns among users' preference for comprehensive attributes across domains. By introducing a new domain-aggregated attribute preference learning task, MSDCR can learn the common attribute preference more effectively. Furthermore, MSDCR employs a multi-graph attention network to aggregate the attribute preferences from multiple domains, as the patterns of users' preference may be correlated across different domains. Experimental evaluations of MSDCR on real-world datasets demonstrate its superior performance of cooperative recommendation in multi-sparse-domain scenarios.

Hitchin's self-intersection formula for stable bundles on a complex algebraic surface can be reinterpreted through the deformation theory of bundles, also incorporating perpendicular and symplectic variants. Specifically, the approach utilizes the relationship between deformation spaces of simple vector bundles and the zero locus of a section on a line bundle. For perpendicular bundles, focusing on extremal bundles yields a deformation-theoretic extension of Hitchin's formula, with the sum of deformation spaces for each charge coinciding with Hitchin's formula. For symplectic bundles, a similar analysis holds, with the sum of deformation spaces for each charge being zero, aligning with Donaldson's result that symplectic bundles have vanishing Chern classes.

Let $a_{n,k}$ denote the number of divisions of $n$ where each part has a multiplicity less than $k$, and the resulting subintervals are also less than $k$. We derive a formula for $a_{n,k}$ and explore the associated generating functions. Specifically, we observe that the associated generating functions exhibit a division at $x^k = 1$. This phenomenon suggests a combinatorial explanation, which in turn leads to the discovery of a particular class of objects, represented by a recursive relationship, that have a one-to-one correspondence with the desired divisions. We express $a_{n,k}$ using a recursive formula and demonstrate that the associated generating functions can be expressed as the product of two simpler generating functions, effectively simplifying the problem.

When generating and collecting data, inevitable imperfections can seriously hinder our ability to derive accurate conclusions. In order to guarantee reliable outcomes, we must first establish that the data we collect is of high enough quality, and then develop a reliable method of estimation. This study provides a framework for ensuring the reliability of data and offers a simple approach to validating the reliability of least squares estimations. To do this, we introduce a concept of relative error tolerance and develop a formula to estimate the likelihood that estimated parameters fall within a predetermined safe margin of error. This framework is versatile, as it enables the extension of traditional least squares validation to data collected in various environments, such as outdoor lighting of any intensity, with or without signal processing. Furthermore, our framework allows the assessment of data quality in mathematical models and the reliability of estimations under prior uncertainty. By applying this framework, we can efficiently determine the required data collection time to ensure reliable parameters, thereby optimizing data collection for resource-constrained systems. Lastly, we illustrate the practical applications of our framework through a series of high-level algorithmic outlines, and demonstrate its versatility via a real-world example in which we validate the reliability of camera calibration.

Using a quark gain-loss approach and considering the effects of color flux tube, we investigate how heavy $c$ and $b$ mesons are produced and move within the quark-gluon plasma at high energies. Our study reveals that the X(3872) distribution is predominantly driven by the $J/\psi$ production in the quark-gluon plasma, with the contribution from quark and antiquark partons being negligible. Additionally, we find that the X(3872) may have a larger production rate than initially estimated and that its forward-forward asymmetry is primarily determined by the $J/\psi$ production in the quark-gluon plasma. Our calculations of the X(3872) differential and integral distributions are presented for both the LHC and RHIC. Our research also obtains the differential and integral distributions of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ heavy charmonium states at the LHC.

The occurrence of local moments is widespread in disordered semiconductor materials, such as silicon doped with phosphorus, and it is seen both when these materials are metallic and when they are insulators. We are focusing specifically on how local moments behave in insulators that have disorder, and we are finding that this behavior originates from repulsive forces between electrons. We are using advanced numerical techniques to investigate models of interacting insulators, including a well-known type of chain called the Hubbard chain, and we are finding specific types of correlations within these models. Our results show that there is an exponential decrease in some correlations and a power-law decrease in others, and we are explaining these findings using a simplified picture that arises when interactions between particles are very strong.

A significant structure within a Coxeter system is a product of its standard parabolic subgroups, each corresponding to a particular height. The foundation theorem, specifically for Coxeter groups of type A, reveals that the highest such subgroups, associated with algebraic Bethe vectors, have distinct characteristics when compared to those of lower-ranking subgroups. Building upon this, we extend the framework of the foundation theorem to B-type Coxeter groups, defining a related concept known as a foundation set. The implicit set, analogous to algebraic Bethe vectors in type A, serves as the basis for our extension.

We develop the soliton profile in a class of interacting scalar field theories characterized by $SO(2)$ invariance, where the scalar field transforms as a bi-doublet under two $SO(3)$ groups, $SO(3)_L$ and $SO(3)_R$. The soliton profile corresponds to a vacuum expectation value of a scalar field that breaks an $SO(2)$ invariance, resulting from the difference in vacuum expectation values of two scalar fields with distinct transformations under the two $SO(3)$ groups. The derivation of the soliton profile follows the method of Gauss' law, where we first solve the classical equation of motion for one of the scalar fields, then use the other field to satisfy Gauss' law, ultimately rescaling the solution to account for arbitrary Dirac observables. The soliton profile in these theories has a significant impact on the interaction between fundamental particles and can be applied to different types of scalar field interactions, as exemplified by our analysis of two models where one allows for an exact solution and the other has a fixed parameter value that must be determined through other methods. Furthermore, the soliton profile in these theories has far-reaching applications in different areas, such as in descriptions of fundamental particle interactions and in models of the early universe where the soliton profile plays a critical role.

Inverse reinforcement learning is a successful technique for automatically learning a reward function from observations of an expert's behavior in scenarios where robots can partially perceive the expert's actions.  A significant challenge in in RL is determining when to update the reward function in response to occasional anomalies observed in the expert's behavior.  Our approach presents a Bayesian framework for learning a noise-reduced estimate of the expert's intended action probabilities.  When new data are integrated, the model adjusts by refining the parameters that govern how the expert's actions translate to observations.  As a result, the model becomes more confident in its estimation of these parameters without being unduly influenced by isolated observations.  Building on this framework, we developed a method for updating the reward function only when the new data are consistent with the existing model.  Our approach was tested in simulations of a robot learning to pick up objects in a 2D environment.

We are focusing on systems that consist of a basic model and a set of perturbations, and the control system's stability is being evaluated based on the similarity between the fundamental group of the set of perturbations and a specific subgroup. This analysis relies on the system's linearization being stable and the existence of a special type of control system structure, known as the linearization stability property. In addition to this, we are considering a specific set of rules, known as the group rules, in order to determine the allowed range of system modifications, or loop transfer regions, that ensure the system's stability under various perturbations. In this context, we are exploring the relationship between the fundamental group of the set of perturbations and a specific subgroup by studying relative loop transfer regions, which are defined as the set of system parameters for which the system's stability is equivalent to the stability of a related system on a smaller scale, and are ultimately generalizing our findings to the entire fundamental group.

To tackle complex control problems, researchers have made significant strides in recent years, thanks to the power of reinforcement learning. Yet, several challenging issues persist in controlling difficult tasks, such as managing partial observability, handling large action spaces, and dealing with sparse rewards. To address these problems, we introduce a novel two-phase reinforcement learning approach that leverages a secondary stage for critical decision-making. By doing so, we significantly improve the performance of existing methods and achieve remarkable results, including complete control over hard tasks like Atari games and complex robotic manipulation tasks.

Our research continues with an extension of the initial paper in the series, focusing on the development of black holes across various epochs. This follow-up study explores how supermassive black holes are formed and how the distribution of black holes changes over time. To achieve this, we extended the initial model to include the growth of supermassive black holes, which significantly altered the mass distribution across different epochs, especially at higher masses. Our results are consistent with observations of galaxy and black hole scaling relations, and we predict a peak in the mass distribution of supermassive black holes at approximately $10^{8}-10^{9}$ M$_{\odot}$, in line with recent findings from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. This follow-up study also examines supermassive black holes that reside within the nuclei of active galaxies, which have masses ranging from $10^{6}$ to $10^{10}$ M$_{\odot}$. To accurately represent the mass distribution of supermassive black holes, we employed a combination of two different functions: a hybrid model that initially includes a power law component for smaller masses and a Gaussian for larger masses. This hybrid model effectively represents the mass distribution of supermassive black holes across different epochs, which further validates its utility in modeling the general black hole mass distribution.

Neural networks are increasingly being used to analyze inelastic neutron scattering data, but due to their lack of transparency, it's often difficult to interpret their results. To address this issue, we explore methods to make neural networks more readable, highlighting their similarities to conventional spectral analysis techniques. By using proportionality constants, we bring the output of our neural network back into line with the actual experimental cross-section measurements. This step is crucial as it corrects a fundamental flaw found in previous studies using neural networks with a sigmoid output. We also present a straightforward approach to determine the uncertainty margins associated with our output, effectively making our neural network a reliable tool for data interpretation and further understanding.

Preprints have experienced significant growth over the past thirty years, facilitated by advances in digital technology and the expanding role of the internet. Since the initial preprint archive was established in 1991, the number of preprints has increased at an exponential rate. Various factors have contributed to this rapid progress, including the creation of arXiv in 1998, which has played a crucial role in shaping the future of digital preprint services. These developments have led to a corresponding increase in the number of researchers submitting preprints, with corresponding advances in citation and impact metrics. Notably, the pandemic of 2020 brought preprints into the mainstream, prompting major funding agencies to endorse and fund preprint initiatives. The subsequent decade has seen continued momentum from established players and novel entrants, with emerging models of preprint service provision. This article presents an overview of digital preprint services from the United States and Europe, highlighting trends and lessons learned, while also exploring potential challenges and opportunities for future growth.

The digital laboratory journal is an essential tool for recording the details of experiments, providing a paper-based safe space for reflection and analysis in an ever-changing scientific environment. This document outlines our plan to create a DIY, open-source digital counterpart, catering to individual students and research institutions alike, as a publicly accessible GitHub project. This digital journal will be developed using Jekyll, a simple and versatile static site generator, to facilitate easy updating and maintenance. Its minimalistic design is deliberately lacking in fancy features to begin with, allowing users to tailor it to their specific needs. This digital laboratory journal is intended to be a collective effort, welcoming contributions from everyone in the scientific community to create a comprehensive and versatile platform.

High-entropy alloys, pushing the boundaries of materials science, offer remarkable performance and resilience despite some inherent limitations. To optimize their properties, there's a pressing need to establish a direct link between their chemical composition, atomic structure, and mechanical properties. To bridge this gap, artificial intelligence techniques can be leveraged, as seen in the latest applications. This study delves into the benefits and obstacles of integrating machine learning into high-entropy alloys research and pinpoints areas of improvement, identifying key hurdles to address. Ultimately, the paper outlines promising avenues for AI to enhance HEA research and opens the door for more cutting-edge materials breakthroughs.

The recent discovery of the $T_{cc}^+$ by the LHCb collaboration is a significant finding as it is the first observed example of a heavy-quark spin triplet partner. We develop a theoretical framework to investigate the decay pattern of the $T_{cc}^+$ to its constituent parts, specifically $D^{\ast}D\pi$. Since the $T_{cc}^+$ is a heavy-quark spin partner, it is governed by rules that are insensitive to quark dynamics, thereby validating the discovered partial decay width of about 1.5-2.9 keV, which is in the range of LHCb's measurement.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks have led to the development of multiple approaches for learning latent structure within data. Despite this progress, there remains a lack of unified theory underlying these methods, which hinders understanding of their inherent limitations and capabilities. This work introduces a novel framework, based on a differential equation, that provides a theoretical foundation for graph neural networks. This framework, known as the "DECGN" model, consists of a graph neural network learning latent variables, accompanied by corresponding equations that maintain consistency with the graph structure. Through statistical analysis, it is proven that certain graph neural networks are capable of modeling complex, dependent data sets while avoiding the formation of cycles. Meanwhile, attempts to extend popular graph neural networks, such as the graph convolutional network, result in models that are only able to learn linear relationships. This work also explores, through numerical simulations, the effects of overparameterization on graph neural networks and identifies a parameter range in which these models can still successfully learn dependent data sets. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that certain graph neural networks can be interpreted as methods for modeling stochastic processes through partial differential equations, similar to established techniques such as the Chen and Cucker method.

We establish the optimal affine dimension for Slim Sidon sets in affine spaces, achieving the result through derivation of a novel estimate for the nonlinearity of vectorial Boolean mappings, which we formulate as a mathematical statement.

Binarized matrices are gaining traction in various data science applications, such as computer vision and machine learning, due to their reduced memory and processing requirements. The challenge lies in their inherent noise caused by matrix binarization, which necessitates efficient sampling methods to approximate matrix rank. Our research focuses on parameter-free approaches for sampling binary matrices based on their geometric properties, specifically the off-diagonal zero constraint. This type of matrix is commonly used in low-rank rank decomposition algorithms. Our experiments demonstrate that sampling binary matrices efficiently is achievable in both exact and approximate scenarios, with the added benefit of being scalable.

I'm proposing the "fitTheOREA" open-source software package, which provides an extensive range of tools to fit and analyze various probability density functions to experimental data, with a particular focus on parton distribution functions. Developed using Python with the PyFit framework, fitTheOREA offers a flexible, adaptable approach that can easily incorporate new fit functions and data. Currently, the package includes support for numerous fit functions, data sets, and nuisance parameters, as well as resonance-based parton distribution functions with fixed-flow and variable-flow options. Furthermore, it incorporates theOREA (Octopus with an adaptive engine), which is an iterative, re-optimization technique that uses different momenta to discover biases in parton distribution functions.

This document outlines the official release of the ELKI data mining framework in version 0.7.5, also known as "Heidelberg". The framework aims to promote interdisciplinary data analysis and research by offering a comprehensive set of statistical, connectivity, clustering, indexing, and supervised learning techniques. The framework supports efficient data analysis for large datasets through its integration of efficient indexing methods, such as the R*-tree. This release marks the first public availability of the framework following two years of development and brings together a vast number of algorithms under a single banner, facilitating easy comparison and combination of techniques.

We investigate parametrically generated light in an elongated microresonator with a linear variation in diameter. The research reveals that, due to its linear profile, the typical four-lobe pattern of parametric solitron radiation is distorted and transformed into a broader spectrum of light as it exits the resonator. Theoretical models are used to explain that this radiation, originating from a stable family of solitons, can take the form of a coherent anti-stokes component when it overlaps with a pump laser, effectively creating a broad optical frequency comb. The model also predicts that changing the resonator's length will alter the parameters of this comb and its spectral characteristics. The study of these variations offers potential opportunities for adjusting the comb's characteristics and improving the coherence of the generated light.

We establish a criterion for determining whether a subgroup within an acylindrically hyperbolic group is loyal, meaning it meets a specific condition in relation to action on a graph. This develops previous research by Druţu and Kapovich who identified loyal subgroups within acylindrically hyperbolic groups. The developed criterion allows for the creation of loyal subgroups within acylindrically hyperbolic groups through a combination of random generation and existence of a specific type of subgroups. This results in the existence of a certain countable group of which every non-identity element generates a loyal subgroup.

Quantization has gained significant interest recently due to its ability to reduce memory, acceleration, and energy consumption of neural networks. This process can be further understood by analyzing the changes it brings to the neural network's intrinsic properties. Previous studies have shown that quantization often results in improved generalization performance, but the underlying reason remains unclear. This study focuses on binary weight neural networks and their nonlinear kernel tensor, examining how they differ from traditional high-precision neural networks. Findings indicate that binary weight networks, despite appearing similar to their full-precision counterparts, actually represent fundamentally distinct types of models. The improvement in generalization performance can be attributed to the " regularization by structural change" effect, where the specific structure of binary weight networks contributes to improved effectiveness. This concept is supported by simulation-based evaluation.

In a black hole perspective, the holographic principle demonstrates that information is entropically ranked by a thermal entropy pyramid. Research has extended this concept to solid state systems, revealing a similar informational hierarchy. This study investigates quantum critical surfaces on the boundaries of phase diagrams, examining their intersection with the thermal entropy pyramid's structure. By analyzing a lattice model of Y-routes in the 3D semiconductor material indium antimonide, this investigation explores how critical surfaces modulate entropy throughout the phase diagram, potentially violating the strict hierarchy imposed by the thermal entropy pyramid.

When a lattice framework's vertices are shifted by vector differences, the resulting points form a new lattice and the original edges intersect at these points, following a specific pattern. The number of times these points intersect can be expressed as the result of a formula involving the framework's features and the lattice's characteristics. By applying a specific technique, the problem of counting these intersection points can be broken down into simpler tasks related to the framework's more regular sublattices. This approach allows us to determine the number of intersection points in a broader range of lattice frameworks than before, including those made up of equal squares, triangles, and other shapes. Even with this expanded range, however, the problem remains challenging for certain types of lattice frameworks, as demonstrated by an example involving the chequerboard pattern.

Signal recovery algorithms for compressed sensing often benefit from regularization techniques, such as extrapolation or relaxation, to stabilize their output and enhance convergence. However, the original methods mentioned above are not actually stabilizing in the context of compressed sensing, it's the incorporation of a stabilizing measure such as the $\ell_1$-norm to counter data noise or regularization over the iterations that yields benefit. 

The goal of this paper is to explore different stabilization methods in compressed sensing which involve an iterative process. Initially, we examine the process of iterative hard thresholding and how incorporating a quantization operator along with the \textit{total-variation} norm leads to robustness in the presence of data noise. 

Furthermore, we develop a new method called iterative soft thresholding of the gradient (ISTG), applicable under circularly symmetric gauge functions, which provides strong stability despite noisy data. Moreover, we generalize the concept of ISTG to cover non-gaussian priors through the introduction of the \textit{Orlitski norm}, which we then specialize in the context of compressed sensing under non-gaussian measurements.

Finally, we demonstrate that our proposed methods are capable of achieving an optimal recovery performance in the presence of noisy data, even in scenarios where the initial signal is far from being perfectly recoverable.

When merging individual frames from various sources, the point spread function's variation across different frames can be a significant factor, affecting the accuracy of the merged image. This is particularly relevant in fringe removal and the processing of fringe video sequences. A plausible model for the point spread function of a merged frame has been formulated. This model distinguishes between two types of PSF structures: those influenced by the location of the frame's fringe minimum and those affected by a point source. The model further includes the concept of a fringe minimum surface (FMS) that maintains consistency across different frames and can be used to calculate the PSF of a merged image. This has been demonstrated through the application of this model to two, experimentally obtained frames, and the resulting point spread functions show noticeable differences, highlighting the need for a more in-depth analysis into the point spread functions of merged images.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field domains under conformal equivalence with respect to a continuous stochastic process evolving in the positive real axis direction. We demonstrate the existence of a mapping that orients imaginary surfaces in the sense of MSAS, establishing their equivalence to a continuum of driven SLE processes governed by a random log-gas process, and proving a conformal equivalence theorem that mirrors aspects of MRS' results.

This research investigates the unique characteristics of solutions to the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional spaces with periodic boundary conditions. We have established that for certain specific initial conditions, the associated solution will remain bounded indefinitely in time when measured against a specific norm, denoted as $\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}_\mu^\alpha$. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the solution can be analytically extended to a domain with a larger parameter of $\mu$ and $\alpha$, providing valuable insights into the properties of solutions in multi-dimensional spaces. Notably, our results differ from those obtained using other methods, such as those involving energy estimates. Moreover, our findings imply that the solution will remain smooth (in the sense of being Holder continuous) for certain specific initial conditions, even when the force acting on the system is smooth. Notably, our results demonstrate that the solution will retain its smoothness (in the sense of being Holder continuous) for certain specific initial conditions, even when the domain is two-dimensional and the viscosity is extremely low.

Quantum computers can perform certain tasks far more efficiently than classical machines, but verifying their output, when it matches the expected result, proves to be a major obstacle, posing an exponential challenge. Researchers have developed verification methods using quantum techniques such as circuit checking, but these require significant resources, rendering them feasible only through substantial investments. This study presents a groundbreaking approach that brings verification efficiency down to linear time, opening up possibilities for practical applications. We utilize specialized properties of specific quantum circuits, transforming the problem into matching binary strings, a task that can be easily automated at a linear scale. The complexity analysis is carefully examined to ensure efficiency without introducing unnecessary complications. The proposed method is thoroughly tested on actual quantum circuit designs, demonstrating its practical value and comparing favorably to current techniques. The development of this algorithm brings us closer to effectively using quantum computers for calculating critical parts of quantum circuit outputs, even when verification becomes a major hurdle.

Generating realistic shapes of growing cells is challenging, especially with varying sizes. A common approach to this problem involves solving partial differential equations (PDEs) that is computationally intensive and difficult to scale up. In this research, we explore implicit neural representations (INRs) as a viable shape generation method due to its ability to produce precise control over shapes and adapt well to large datasets. INRs achieve state-of-the-art results in synthesizing cell shapes of considerable size without overfitting, according to established metrics. Furthermore, INRs allow for the learning of cell wall patterns, an essential feature of plant cell development. By leveraging INRs, we can generate cell shapes with controllable properties, such as curvature and surface area, which is beneficial for shaping three-dimensional cell structures. INRs also facilitate the synthesis of missing data in incomplete cell models and support training of shape-level tasks through supervision. The benefits of INRs extend to real-world applications, including validating cell shape hypotheses and guiding the development of cell-shaped robots.

The underlying map theory, a concept that began in the late 1950s, posits that rats learn the layout of their environment through reinforcement learning, using mental maps like the grid cell system. However, this idea has been challenged by some experimental results seemingly contradicting the map theory. To address these discrepancies, our group proposed a reinterpretation of the map theory, referred to as the "sampled map theory." This reformulated perspective posits that rats learn and remember the location of key events, such as finding food, rather than a comprehensive mental map of their environment. According to the sampled map theory, these episode locations are represented by a dynamic and adaptable spatial memory, akin to random walk paths, where proximity in mental space approximates physical proximity. Our machine learning model, trained using a reinforcement learning-based algorithm, demonstrates similar performance to that of rats when presented with novel situations, showcasing the sampled map theory's predictive capabilities.

In the domain of continuous-time Markov chains, a significant distinction can be drawn between those that adhere to retrograde dynamics and those that defy this constraint. Utilizing a transition matrix analysis, we identify key characteristics that differentiate these types of chains, leading to a concept of 'hard-drive dipoles', which serve as a tangible representation of the difference, and subsequently introduce the notion of 'hard-drive semicircles' as a symbolic representation, thereby establishing a visual framework for distinguishing non-retrograde Markov chains.

The research of Sound Event Detection (SED) aims to pinpoint and identify acoustic phenomena in an audio record. In this study, we employ a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) using rectangular filters to enhance SED performance. By addressing the limitations of previous studies, such as low overall accuracy and poor recall in specific classes, we boost the mainline accuracy and substantially improve the recall of source classes like "car horn." A novel enhancement technique is proposed by integrating data augmentation through channel rotation. Evaluation of various channel rotation strategies suggests that using all four channel orientations is more effective than confining the augmentation to upper or lower frequency ranges. Moreover, we introduce a new ground truth annotation for "car horn," allowing for a notable improvement in its detection recall from 18.43% to 52.98%.

Concurrent transmission based wireless systems, like VLC and millimeter wave systems, have distinct transmission methods: VLC uses a highly directed approach, while millimeter wave systems leverage high frequency yet short range transmission. Current technology relies on systems with a single active transmission path, but future technologies like 6G might enable thousands of simultaneous transmissions. This requirement poses significant challenges to existing network architectures, necessitating new design approaches. This paper conducts a thorough assessment of concurrent transmission based wireless systems, highlighting their unique complexities and limitations. Further, it explores the potential of these systems in addressing 6G's persistent challenges, such as high resolution sensing, intelligent control, and seamless coexistence. This overview also delves into the potential of these systems in addressing these issues and provides a framework for implementing these concepts.

The significance of stochastic processes in modeling real-world phenomena has been increasingly recognized. This growing recognition has sparked a new approach to signal examination, which considers inherent randomness in signals. This approach is distinguished from traditional signal processing methods that use deterministic stochastic processes to analyze noise. Our stochastic geometry method for analyzing signal patterns relies on the geometric properties of the underlying probability measures of spectrogram level contours, providing a complete and consistent description of the signal. This technique is employed to develop a novel interpretation of the Kullback-Leibler divergence measure, along with a way to quantitatively assess the similarity of two signals. This similarity assessment is inspired by recent advancements in the visualization of stochastic processes, which have enabled the representation of a pair of mutually consistent stochastic processes through a shared geometric structure.

We developed a two-pronged approach to identify multiple patterns of behavior in complex networks of spiking neurons, specifically where groups of neurons perform similar patterns of activity at different times. Our approach first uses a technique to detect and characterize these patterns, and then uses another method to identify any changes occurring within these patterns over time. To help ensure our results are accurate, we use a measure to gauge how well our methods match the expected outcomes from theoretical analyses. By using this approach on various examples of networks, we were able to successfully detect chimeric states and groups of synchronized neurons, and further analyze these patterns to understand their dynamics. Given the complexity of these systems and the various forms they can take, as well as the different methods used to study them, we believe our approach contributes positively to the field by providing a reliable set of tools to analyze and understand these systems, and by highlighting the differences between different methods to stimulate further research and comparison. It is available at https://arxiv.org/doi/ark:/arxiv:2003.00723.

The random force method, initially designed for turbulent molecular dynamics, has been adapted and tested for celestial mechanics involving $N$ bodies in a new version of the REBOUND code. This method involves generating random forces that slow down orbiting objects, achieving the desired collision probability by adjusting a parameter based on the collision frequency of the $N$ bodies. The REBOUND version incorporating the random force method is highly efficient, with a low-memory requirement, and works effectively for a wide range of scenarios from simple two-body encounters to 34-body simulations, making it suitable for Celestial Mechanics and planetology applications.

Continuous feedback regulation is a crucial technique for stabilizing linear and nonlinear quantum systems in the presence of Markovian damping. Our study provides a comprehensive approach to analyzing systems governed by the quantum Fokker-Planck equation, with a particular focus on developing tools for precise feedback designs. We establish a fundamental operator expression for the maximum entropy Bayesian estimator and, using it, derive a solution to the optimal feedback problem subject to a specific constraint on the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. This operator expression is shown to be amenable to numerical computation, and we illustrate its applicability with three examples: the quantum Brownian motion in the presence of a heat bath, a laser-like quantum system with solvent particles, and a system consisting of a focal point dynamically coupled to a wave, allowing for the adjustment of coupling strength via a control point.

For a two-dimensional disk assembly packed in a channel with random obstacles, we studied the steady-state configurations of masses in a channel with even and odd sequences of obstacles. By applying periodic boundary conditions, we analyzed the large-system limits of these configurations. Our research revealed specific pressure profiles for these scenarios, along with the associated correlation functions. Additionally, we examined the possibility of obtaining constant flow rates in these assemblies by identifying the appropriate imbalance of pressure head and shear stress.

Research into El Ni\~no's distinct forms has concentrated on their impacts on the environment, yet their influence on local climate patterns, particularly the unusual seasonal precipitation patterns in parts of the world like South Africa and India, is largely unexplored. To this end, the various forms of El Ni\~no have been studied for their effect on seasonal precipitation patterns in East Africa, India, Southern Africa, and East Asia using Earth System Model simulations. The analysis found distinct patterns of precipitation associated with each form of El Ni\~no in specific regions. For example, in East Africa, certain types of El Ni\~no lead to above-average precipitation in key areas, while in India, the relationship between certain types of El Ni\~no and precipitation in the country's central region is particularly notable. The models show that the relationship between certain types of El Ni\~no and precipitation in this region is particularly strong. The research highlights the potential for the models to identify regions vulnerable to above-average, below-average, or varying precipitation patterns during different types of El Ni\~no, which could inform adaptation and climate-resilience efforts in several countries.

The formation process of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) is not yet fully understood, particularly at the lower end of the mass spectrum. A new theoretical approach, known as "Massive Black Hole Binary Formation Pathways," has been developed to explain this process, and recent discoveries of low-mass SMBHs have provided support for these pathways. However, further evidence is needed to confirm that one of these pathways, designated as "Pathway 1," is responsible for SMBH formation. Pathway 1 involves a central SMBH that forms a binary with another SMBH, and in many cases, a large amount of gas and dust accumulates around the binary, eventually leading to a merger that results in an even larger SMBH. In most scenarios, a significant amount of gas and dust remains unprocessed and forms a large accretion disk around the new SMBH, which would be visible through ultraviolet and optical observations. In contrast, a massive SMBH that forms through another pathway, known as "Pathway 3," does not have such a prominent accretion disk, as it is thought to have formed through stellar mergers. A extensive search for low-mass SMBHs has been conducted, and a recent discovery of a low-mass SMBH in the dwarf galaxy Leo I has provided a new opportunity to test whether Pathway 1 is responsible for SMBH formation. In the quantum materials field, flat bands in low-dimensional structures are particularly interesting because of their potential to harbor flat bands. These flat bands can lead to the localization of charge carriers at very low temperatures and induce unusual correlations that can be beneficial for understanding the properties of quantum materials. Flat bands have been found to influence the magnetic properties of a few materials, but not their electrical resistance, until now. A new study has discovered that it is possible to suppress the electrical resistance of a kagome compound by tuning a external magnetic field, providing a new perspective on the relationship between flat bands and unusual magnetism. Using ultra-high magnetic field facilities, researchers found that increasing magnetic field can trigger a phase transition and reduce electrical resistance by one to two orders of magnitude, depending on the sample structure. These findings include the improvement of antiferromagnetic ordering, the formation of a superconducting state, and the activation of a quantum fluctuation phase that is hard to reach at zero magnetic field. These observations demonstrate the intricate relationship between flat bands, magnetism, and electrical resistance, and reveal the potential for external magnetic fields to manipulate this interaction.

The surge in publicly available genomic data through various projects and research initiatives has made it possible to apply machine learning techniques to a range of interesting human traits. We have explored the application of genomic information in learning patterns through dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA and t-SNE, demonstrating the efficacy of collaborative data sharing and analysis. Building upon this understanding, we have also utilized genomic information to investigate the connections between specific characteristics and genetic variations through genome-wide association studies. Our results indicate that functional genomic data can be leveraged to improve the identification of associated genetic variations. Specifically, our analysis revealed key associations between certain functional regions and traits such as height, metabolic rate, and sleep duration, while our comparison of different annotation approaches enabled the selection of the most relevant sets of genomic regions for further investigation. Ultimately, our findings illustrate the value of integrating genomic information and facilitating data sharing among institutions in order to gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between human characteristics and their underlying genomic basis.

We have identified and categorized the block systems of Seymour's chordal graphs that have a cyclic group action, consisting of those that remain unchanged under reflection and those that don't. It was found that the group action on these systems can be either cyclic, dihedral, or abelian (with two or more components), with the systems falling into one of six possible forms, and also that the systems with cyclic group action are exactly those represented by the graph classes of line graphs, oriented line graphs, and circular graphs. Additionally, it was discovered that the general linear group acts transitively on the projective line graph's block system when the underlying graph is bipartite, with the action being non-flags-transitive in general but admitting local non-flags-transitive in specific cases. Furthermore, a list has been provided of all line graphs whose group action on blocks is cyclic, with also being flags-transitive. Also, a list has been given of all oriented line graphs whose group action on blocks is cyclic, with also being flags-transitive. Moreover, it has been found that the group action on the circular graph's block system can either be a dihedral or an abelian group. With regard to oriented line graphs, it has been found that the group action on the block system can either be a dihedral or an abelian group with two components (with the result also extending to circular graphs).
