Researchers have introduced an innovative technique for determining the masses of short-lived nuclei using a cyclotron-type mass spectrometer. This method leverages the unique characteristics of isochronous acceleration to precisely measure the masses of these nuclei. By analyzing the momentum ratios of ions with half-lives, scientists can calculate the mass differences with superior precision. Experimental validation of this technique was achieved through the development of a specialized detector system. Application of this technique to niobium isotopes demonstrated its potential for high-precision mass measurements.

The concept of quantum flow provides a versatile framework for studying latent structures within quantum field theories, offering more subtle insights than perturbation theory, and a growing body of research is exploring its applications in lattice field theory. To fully utilize the information present in the continuum limit, standardized quantum flows are necessary, and we demonstrate their implementation in one-loop perturbation theory. Our work serves as a guideline for standardized flows on a lattice, and we illustrate their application with examples in $\phi^4$ theory, both with and without the inclusion of gauge interactions.

This research focuses on improving the recognition of structured text, found commonly in IDs, addresses, names, and dates. A novel approach is presented, consisting of a direct recognition model and a pattern-favoring model. The pattern-favoring model is designed to prefer results that conform to predefined regular expressions, effectively serving as a pre-filter to enhance the overall accuracy. A comprehensive dataset, consisting of 26,000 labeled items in various formats, is utilized to train and evaluate both models. The findings suggest that the combination of the two models surpasses the performance of current commercial services and the standalone model in structured text recovery. Moreover, the proposed technique demonstrates the ability to rectify errors made by the standalone model, even when the incorrect result is close to the correct one. In particular, the progress in reading utility bill IDs and postal codes is notable. The project's code and the specialized toolkit for generating regular expression favoring models are made available online for further exploration.

The production of 135 charged and neutral top quark pairs in 89.8 inverse microbarn proton-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV was measured using the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC. Unlike lead-lead collisions, where a significant nuclear bias is observed, these proton-lead collisions show no notable variation in same-sign dilepton events. Additionally, same-sign and opposite-sign dimuon production in the same pseudorapidity range exhibits comparable yields, with notable differences in mass distribution patterns observed. These findings demonstrate that nuclear biases in same-sign dilepton events are distinctly linked to charge signs. Furthermore, cross-section measurements of top quark production in proton-lead collisions are consistent with theoretical predictions, with measured cross-sections in both charged and neutral top quark pairs showing acceptable agreement with predictions.

This study focuses on the key elements of text-to-SQL tasks, specifically the ability of models to grasp semantic relationships and perform precise matching of text data. To evaluate this, we developed the SEM-MT, a new task to measure the similarity between text semantics, drawn from existing benchmarks and generated for our purposes. The use of this new task allows us to assess the semantic matching capability of text-to-SQL models. Moreover, we identified a common issue among existing text-to-SQL models: they struggle to perform matching operations on text data. To address this, we introduced a novel input format modification method that significantly improves the performance of text-to-SQL models. Finally, our analysis shows that enhancing text-to-SQL models with semantic matching capabilities via a auxiliary task improves both overall performance and match performance.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the large-scale environment influences galaxy evolution. Recent findings reveal that noise in wide-area radio surveys impact bias calculations, resulting in varying bias estimates as radio depth increases. To mitigate this issue, the LoTSS data team developed a method to account for noise when determining x-ray luminosity bias. To further refine these estimates, the team conducted additional simulations to derive theoretical bias values to compare with data. Applying the corrected bias calculations to the LoTSS data yields consistent results for x-ray luminosity and stellar mass bias estimates. Furthermore, by analyzing the LoTSS data, the team found no significant evidence of significant non-linear bias variation among different galaxy morphology types. With more LoTSS data sets anticipated to arrive in the forthcoming data releases, the team plans to extend their analysis to investigate further aspects of galaxy evolution.

The Ranking Lasso (RL) is a key problem in data analysis that involves selecting the most relevant features from a high-dimensional dataset. Solving this problem directly is challenging because it involves non-convex constraints and the computational time is proportional to the number of data points. To overcome this limitation, an alternative formulation, High-Dimensional Ranking Lasso (HDL), is proposed, which allows for more efficient feature selection using convex optimization methods. However, the proposed methods in the original paper prove to be impractical due to excessive computational times. In response, an alternative adaptive-sieving-based algorithm, IASP, is introduced to tackle the HDL problem. The new algorithm leverages adaptive-sieving techniques to efficiently handle the high-dimensional nature of the problem, resulting in significantly improved computational times. Specifically, the number of iterations is proportional to the number of features, rather than the number of data points, making it much more practical. The proposed algorithm, IASP, is further validated by comparing it to various existing methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, which demonstrates its superior performance in terms of accuracy and speed.

The requirement for a system to be close to equilibrium as compared to its characteristic relaxation time is examined in more detail for two distinct types of driving forces. It is discovered that, unlike uniform driving, localized driving can lead to a decrease in the entropy production rate when the driving speed exceeds the characteristic relaxation time. This phenomenon is accompanied by a shift toward lower entropy in the system, indicating a convex entropy production rate-smooth driving speed relationship. Additionally, it has been proven that, regardless of the driving mechanism, a system must be in a metastable state to exhibit this convex property.

AI solutions are widely viewed as a way to achieve environmental sustainability, yet the resources required to develop and utilize them are often disregarded in assessments of their ecological effects. Focusing on renewable energy-based AI data centers, this study explores the previously overlooked energy pathways of AI systems. It involves analyzing existing literature and conducting life cycle assessments to determine the ecological impacts associated with AI development. This approach allows for evaluating the relative benefits of renewable energy-based AI systems in reducing their ecological footprint.

One major challenge facing industrial teams implementing business process management systems is the difficulty in translating the benefits of the literature into practical results. Our recent BPM 2019 Challenge aimed to bridge this gap by identifying effective methods for real-process improvement, and this paper provides a comprehensive update on the methods employed by the winning teams. The update showcases a range of analytical techniques and data visualisation options that can enhance process understanding. However, the underlying issue remains that these methods struggle to recommend practical process changes. Our investigation reveals that the key obstacles include a limited process duration, poorly captured exceptional cases, and a lack of context-specific knowledge. Ultimately, the success of business process management depends on prescriptive techniques that can accurately forecast and guide decisions, and we propose several future directions for BPM system implementation and research.

Advanced manufacturing via heated substance processing demands precise temperature control over a wide range of scales, from individual particles to collections of millions.  A novel algorithm enhances the precision of heated substance processing by reducing temperature errors, even when goal targets are diverse and challenging to achieve. This technique works with a broad model that incorporates the effects of flow, heat, and solidification. A system of abstract goals is established, defined by collective variables that help minimize their discrepancies with desired targets. As goals are adjusted, the algorithm updates the simulation in the direction of optimal performance. This technique was successfully demonstrated in two challenging heated substance processing applications - the removal of impurities using hydrodynamic flushing and the removal of impurities using natural convection - resulting in significantly improved results, particularly when the goal-focused algorithm is combined with goal modulation, leading to near-optimal convection, even in the absence of goal modulation. This technique offers a versatile approach for general-purpose heated substance processing applications, providing a pathway for estimating optimal processing parameters.

A significant challenge in bioinformatics, particularly membrane protein structure prediction, has been resolved through a solution that employs combinatorial optimization and identifies feasible sub-problems via specific criteria, reducing the associated algorithmic complexity. This breakthrough demonstrates the capability of reducing the computational time of certain problems related to membrane protein mapping, from exponential to polynomial time, once certain conditions are met. This paper presents various kernelization algorithms for problems associated with mapping trans-membrane proteins. Kernelization is a technique used to reduce the size of an instance of a problem, obtaining a new instance with at most linear dimensions, while preserving the equivalence of solutions. This study shows that each of the considered problems can be solved efficiently using polynomial time, even with additional constraints, while its equivalent kernelization algorithm runs in linear time. This has implications for fixed-parameter tractility of these problems. Furthermore, the study provides experimental validation for obtained kernels through various paradigms, such as TDZD, FPT, and EXPT.

Individuals may express more extreme opinions in their assessments of social issues when compared to their personal beliefs, a phenomenon known as "limited confidence." This discrepancy can be demonstrated through a mathematical model that considers a person's static opinion as well as their dynamic behavior within a societal framework. By incorporating a parameter that reflects a person's willingness to take a stance, a collective behavior model can be developed to show that as this parameter increases, people's opinions become more polarized, leading to a social consensus, thus illustrating how a distribution of moderate opinions can give rise to a variety of social opinions, including the extremes.

Inside an asymptotically flat, level hairy black hole, the laws of black hole physics continue to hold strong. Our investigation focuses on a recently identified asymptotically flat, level hairy black hole solution, where the mass and charge are evenly distributed across the event horizon in a constant state. In this setting, we have accurately calculated the density and the pressure exerted on the event horizon. Furthermore, we have formally established the laws governing black hole dynamics, including the expansion of the event horizon, junction conditions, and consistent prescription for computing the mass associated with the Hairy Black object. In this process, we have formally established the relationship between mass, charge, and angular momentum, addressing any potential ambiguities associated with the mass computation. Our analysis has confirmed that the mass associated with the Hairy Black object is equal to the sum of its ADM mass and the gravitational potential energy exerted by the ambient fields, in agreement with the principles outlined by Wald and Zurek.

The length of time it takes for a cell to start translating a newly transcribed RNA sequence into protein is a question that has not been fully answered. Despite significant advances in our understanding of RNA synthesis and degradation, this delay, known as the lag period, has yet to be directly measured in a comprehensive study that includes multiple cell types. A model for transcription has been developed which aligns with experimental findings when a certain rate of RNA synthesis is applied consistently across the genome. This delay was estimated to be around 15 minutes based on a study of chicken erythrocytes and was found to be relatively consistent with a previously proposed theory. An adjustment has also been made to account for variations in RNA levels at different lengths for a more accurate estimation of this delay. A test of this model was also conducted which revealed that certain sequences promote a shorter lag period and as a result, higher levels of mature RNA. A comparison of transcription patterns across chicken and mouse cells has also been made which has provided further insight into these processes as well as potential differences between these species. A broader application of this model has also been proposed which could aid in understanding alternative modes of RNA synthesis and the effects of external stimuli on these processes.

Researchers discovered that 64Ni exhibits two 0+ isotopic phases at zero spin, which can be attributed to the influence of a monopole tensor interaction. The application of a monopole tensor interaction, which governs how nucleons interact with each other, to the nuclear shell model reveals that it plays a crucial role in shaping the 0+ phase diagram. The final phase structure is refined through the analysis of computational data, which includes the calculation of energy gaps using the discrete density functional theory.

Chiral gauge theories are interesting variants of gauge theories because of their unique space-time and fermion properties. In particular, they offer great potential for complex and intriguing boundary conditions, which can be consistent with both Grassmannian and bosonic types. Due to their distinct characteristics, chiral gauge theories pose a significant challenge for superstring theory, as they cannot be modeled effectively with any orientifold construction. As a result, they have sparked much debate about their relationship to supersymmetric dualities. Specifically, some chiral gauge theories are proposed to have non-supersymmetric counterparts in fundamental string theory, which are thought to be established through supersymmetry-breaking operations. In this discussion, we will explore the concept of chiral gauge theories and some theoretical models that may serve as candidates for these non-supersymmetric dualities.

A particular type of error-correcting code known as a group code is used in this research, and we focus on developing a specific type of pairing known as a linear complementary set for these codes, using a specific type of mathematical system known as a Galois ring for its underlying finite field.

Graphical models have broadened our understanding of various complex phenomena by introducing a concise mathematical representation of relationships, which can be analyzed using algorithms. While high-efficiency algorithms exist for some applications, others, like exact MPE and optimization under strict constraints, still require substantial computational resources. In this research, we present a new, more efficient representation of probabilistic models, which allows for faster exact MPE calculation and constraint optimization. Our approach also simplifies the analysis of consistency in such models, while still maintaining a reasonable computational load. This representation introduces a new concept, 'equivalence sets', which group equivalent situations within a probabilistic model and provide a more organized structure for handling complex phenomena. Our proposed algorithm, 'brief', identifies equivalence sets and can leverage their analysis to efficiently solve MPE and optimization tasks under strict constraints. Interestingly, 'brief' also offers a simpler alternative to consistance checking, which still guarantees the correctness of results. Our experimental results demonstrate the significant performance boost offered by 'brief', when compared to existing solutions. For example, 'brief' achieves a remarkable speed-up of over 100 times on molecular networks and graphical models of data analysis. Furthermore, 'brief' provides a substantial improvement of up to 20 times in optimization tasks under strict constraints. Our research also highlights the potential of 'brief' to be incorporated into existing computational tools for predictive modeling, with a notable example of its integration into a basic classifier, which results in a 2-3 times faster model.

When a person drops an item, sounds are produced and visual cues appear almost simultaneously. The timing and coordination of these sensory inputs provides crucial information that systems using predictive models or artificial intelligence can exploit to determine whether an event has occurred. In this research, we investigate this phenomenon and develop methods to enhance the detection of dropped items by synchronizing audio and video signals. The study's primary contribution lies in our proposed framework, which uses advanced signal processing techniques and learning algorithms to refine the estimation of drop instant and to incorporate the anticipated sound waveform that would correspond to that drop instant. Experimental results based on simulated data indicate that the proposed method can accurately identify drops even in the presence of background noise, and that it outperforms existing audio and video-based approaches by 5% and 11% respectively. Furthermore, we find that the proposed method can successfully identify drops in real-world videos, and that its performance compares favorably to existing approaches.

Viscosities of various systems, ranging from mixtures of Newtonian fluids to the most complex materials, exhibit unique non-Newtonian characteristics. A particular phenomenon, shear thickening, occurs when a fluid's viscosity increases at higher shear rates, yet unexpectedly becomes extreme in extremely dilute polymer solutions and complex materials, often causing them to solidify under sufficient stress. Despite its significance in both practical and industrial applications to prevent settling, spillage, and irreversible deformation, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of shear thickening does not exist. In order to bridge the gap between experimental observations and theoretical knowledge, we provide an overview of the global scaling of shear thickening transitions, focusing on the power-law velocity profiles that govern this behavior in both simple and complex materials.

Electrical power use can be predicted by first understanding the patterns of power consumption at different times. This research employs Bayesian nonparametric mixing models to analyze hourly electricity usage patterns in Ghana's context, utilizing a variable selection method that assesses the suitability of various distributions. Our findings reveal that a combination of three distributions effectively captures the hourly patterns of electricity usage, replicating the observed patterns with notable accuracy. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that power consumption follows diurnal and seasonal patterns, corroborating findings from existing studies.

The study examines how much relevant information may be missed in Google's Web search results due to personalization. Although previous research suggested that personalized results can lead to overlook relevant results, this study seeks to provide a direct answer to the question: how many relevant results may be missed. To address this question, the researchers created 42 distinct research scenarios, focusing on eight topics, and analyzed the correlation between search queries, both actual and simulated, in two distinct databases: the index database, which is similar to Google's, and a complementary database. The analysis revealed that, on average, as many as 29% of relevant results may be overlooked in personalized searches, with a significant range of between 10% and 64%. Notably, the underlying documents themselves, rather than the search queries, primarily determined the overlook rate. The researchers proposed two factors to predict the overlook rate: the diversity of search queries and the degree of overlap between the index database and the underlying document collection. Based on these findings, the researchers recommended adjusting Google's algorithm either by reducing reliance on past search history or by implementing a simplified algorithm that would yield more comprehensive results for popular search queries.

Automatically creating a program from a visual representation is a complex challenge known as program synthesis. A novel approach to this problem is employed, where a neural network is trained to generate a program by analyzing a flow diagram, by identifying the graph structure, and then recognizing patterns within it. A unique convolutional neural network technique is introduced that processes graph data, along with an analysis of various graph representation methods. The analysis considers multiple criteria to determine the best graph representation for program synthesis. The findings of this study show that a specific representation method produces the highest success rate, at 74.8%, when evaluated using a widely adopted metric. The underlying dataset comprises 5000 flow diagrams, and the convolutional neural network's performance surpasses that of non-neural network methods, such as the 'downhill' approach, which has a significantly lower success rate of 23.2%. Furthermore, when the graph structure is distorted by adding new nodes or edges, the success rate significantly drops to 10.8%, which highlights the importance of an accurate graph structure in program synthesis. A characterization matrix, used to process edge information, is found to be the most effective feature in program synthesis. The study offers insights into utilizing graph representations in program synthesis and provides a framework for using a neural network to generate programs from visual representations.

Our research focuses on how past achievements in dimension reduction can drive future breakthroughs in understanding climate dynamics. This report summarizes recent advancements in this area, highlighting connections between dimension reduction and other climate research topics such as sensitivity, variability, and multiple solutions. It also explores the interplay between methodological developments and theoretical breakthroughs, emphasizing the need for improved dimension reduction tools to advance climate research. Specifically, we're investigating how dimension reduction can be utilized to study climate system sensitivity, multiple equilibria, and complex climate transitions.

The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy, and it coincided with the emergence of kilonovae as a new class of transient objects. Kilonovae, characterized by their short duration and infrared brightness, are created by the fast-moving, relativistic outflows produced by neutron star collisions. Although kilonovae offer an exceptional opportunity to explore the extreme environment of compact objects, the limited wavelength range of electromagnetic observation has made it challenging to thoroughly analyze the ejected material. Nevertheless, the rapid advancement of computer technologies and the development of advanced relativistic many-body theory have enabled researchers to accurately model and compute the optical and neu-tral atomic properties of rare earth elements under extreme conditions. Specifically, our study comprises a systematic calculation of the energy levels, radial profiles, and absorption coefficients of the 4f- and 5s-5p-excited states of Au+IV isoelectronic sequence, utilizing the relativistic atomic structure code by maximizing energy consistency with experimental data and encompassing all possible orbital configurations. The comprehensive data sets of Au+IV and the preceding Os isoelectronic sequence (Os+V-VI) can serve as fundamental reference points for future astrophysical observations, and we believe they will significantly contribute to the ongoing understanding and analysis of kilonova ejecta in the Os to Pt region of the periodic table.

The GI tract begins with the mouth and ends with the anus, and its interior walls undergo dynamic changes due to motility disorders. Such changes complicate clinical assessment and treatment but also create opportunities for improved patient care through personalized therapy. However, these changes also pose significant challenges to accurately tracking the upper and lower GI tracts in video endoscopy footage. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed computer-assisted techniques for upper and lower GI tract segmentation using deep learning, which is a type of machine learning method. Despite the potential of these techniques to aid in clinical assessments and treatments, they are still in the initial stages of development. Our group has been working on creating a fully automated system that employs deep learning to accurately identify the upper and lower boundaries of the GI tract in video endoscopy footage. In our most recent study, we utilized a convolutional neural network to develop an algorithm capable of accurately segmenting the GI tract boundaries in mere milliseconds. Our results indicate substantial progress towards this goal, which we hope will contribute to the development of novel clinical applications.

To analyze complex compositions, such as materials with multiple constituent substances, we employ a structured study approach, centered on a composition vector. By treating this vector as a geometric object, we can perform various transformations and calculations using a systematic method, ensuring consistency and accuracy. Building upon this framework, we develop a step-by-step analysis process for composition data, incorporating statistical analysis, data visualization, and linear problem-solving techniques. Our comprehensive system is designed to be universally applicable and adaptable to high-dimensional data sets, providing a clear and straightforward methodology for addressing a wide range of composition-related problems.

The habitability of exoplanets, particularly those similar in size to Earth, has piqued the interest of astronomers. Previous research suggested that a 'desert' of small, terrestrial planets was found around stars with masses similar to the sun, especially within a specific range (0.25-0.5 M_jupiter). However, this phenomenon was primarily identified through Charrocke-like analysis of Kepler data. This study aimed to explore this 'desert' around similar stars using HARPS/CORALIE data. By utilizing these datasets and applying machine learning algorithms to detect planetary candidates, the researchers searched for potential terrestrial planets. Interestingly, no 'desert' of small, terrestrial planets was found around stars with masses similar to the sun in this particular dataset. Instead, suitable targets for future focused surveys were identified.

To handle the inherent ambiguity in multiple semantic interpretations, Attention models were modified with a cross-bolt regularization method which counteracts over-attention on specific features by compensating for the predictive information lost due to attention-weighting. This cross-bolt regularization uses a contrastive prediction technique to favour representations with more diverse information and increases the robustness of attention networks. Experimental validation was performed on Machine Translation, Image Captioning and Text-to-Speech tasks, and the results demonstrate the improved stability of these models under adversarial conditions.

The Compressed Dark Matter (CDM) model, a simplified scenario where a dark boson $\phi$ acts as a mediator for dark matter interactions with a given coupling to Standard Model particles, has been explored. CDM models are primarily chosen due to the soft boundary where the dark boson mass and coupling intersect, making direct detection more feasible. A recent investigation into CDM models with a Yukawa interaction as the mechanism for dark matter particle decay has been conducted. This analysis demonstrated that, in the context of a Yukawa interaction, the CDM model boundary is not as clearly defined as in the standard kinetic mixing case. A comprehensive search for CDM models with a Yukawa interaction employing mono-$b$ jet plus missing transverse momentum events has been carried out with 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of LHC data. This study established a combined limit on CDM and spin-dependent dark matter scattering for the $pp\to \ell\phi b$ process, with a focus on the $b$ jet being tagged as a $J/\psi$ meson. Additionally, separate limits on CDM and double-differential limits on spin-dependent dark matter scattering have been determined for the $pp\to \ell\phi b$ and $pp\to \nu\phi b$ processes. Neural networks learned through backpropagation were previously compared to biological neurons, revealing significant differences, which subsequently led to the development of novel learning algorithms inspired by biological characteristics. Despite the numerous advantages of these algorithms, their performance in tackling real-world cognitive tasks remains largely untested. To bridge this gap, we evaluated the performance of sparsely connected recurrent neural networks in learning to solve a variety of cognitive tasks related to perception, action, and decision-making. We found that these algorithms can learn to solve multiple tasks more efficiently than other established methods, and their simplified architecture actually facilitates their understanding, which could lead to new insights into how neurons work together.

We present a comprehensive method to classify nilpotent algebras based on their connected components, similar to the classification of nilpotent Lie algebras. Our approach identifies and analyzes the different geometric types of connected nilpotent algebras, and it can be applied to various types of algebras over a field of characteristic not two, and further extended to a broader context.

Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly outshine the entire galaxy, and their numbers peak at a redshift of around 3. Studying these jets in conjunction with the cosmic background radiation allows scientists to gain insight into the processes occurring in the hearts of these galaxies. In order to assess the impact of the cosmic background radiation on jet formation in galaxies at high redshifts, researchers have developed a theoretical model and performed numerical simulations. At a redshift of over 5.5, the model suggests that electrons emitting energy in the form of synchrotron radiation would need to have initial velocities exceeding the speed of light, which is not feasible. However, at a redshift of around 3, the model indicates that gas within the accretion disk would need to be cooler than typical, which is realistic. Moreover, the model suggests that feedback from jets would need to be less efficient in galaxies at a redshift of 3 compared to those at a redshift of 3.5, which has implications for the development of these galaxies. In particular, if the efficiency of jets is similar across all redshifts, the model indicates that galaxies at a redshift of 3 would be heavier than those at a redshift of 3.5, which has consequences for the development of these galaxies. Four distinct Lagrangians that describe classical gravity are presented, each formulated within the context of a Lorentzian manifold. These Lagrangians are specifically designed to yield the Einstein field equations when applied to any manifold, thereby encompassing general relativity as a natural subset. Furthermore, we discuss the Einstein-Hilbert action, highlighting its sensitivity to coordinate transformations and the implications for variational principles in general relativity.

Our approach to imaging research combines 3D techniques with discrete symmetry to create efficient algorithms, as demonstrated by recent developments including efficient matching of 3D images and features, as well as registration of 3D image datasets. Building on previous work, we enhance these algorithms by applying a novel discrete symmetry to the 3D Shortt approximation of the Fourier transform, as well as extending the application of SP-Symmetry to the 3D features of volumes. Additionally, we introduce a novel method for reducing the complexity of binary volumes, as required for efficient feature extraction and registration of these volumes. Experimental results confirm the computational efficiency of our dual-SP approach, as well as its high level of accuracy in both external and self-registration of synthetic and real image datasets.

We conducted an in-depth examination of the highly variable double star system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, which exhibits unusually short and intense eclipse events lasting around 40.5 minutes surrounded by overall system variability. Our detailed analysis of the overall system behavior across ultraviolet to optical wavelengths has allowed us to accurately measure the central star size and the overall system period, along with the pattern and intensity of the primary eclipse events. Our research reveals that the overall system period is 40.495 days, and the central star size is approximately 76 Earth radii. Furthermore, we observed a noticeable rise in UV flux levels approximately 2-3 days before each primary eclipse event, and propose several possible explanations for these increased UV readings including the presence of circumbinary rings and accretion disc formation. Additionally, we observed a noticeable difference in the overall system variability patterns between UV and longer wavelength observations, and the overall system behavior matches the expected patterns for a certain type of binary star system, and the central star size matches the expected range for a particular type of star.

A recent technique called aggregation fusion was proposed for estimating large-scale variables from multiple lower-scale observations, essentially acting as a globalization method. In this study, the technique is scrutinized by equating it to a variational problem related to optimal transport. Our findings reveal that fusion aggregation essentially estimates a global variable that is optically linked to multiple local alternatives. Furthermore, we demonstrate that global aggregation tends to favor smoother estimates and, in cases of close local estimates, it aspirates to be a perfect forecaster. Our analysis also reveals that global aggregation is affected by issues of existence and uniqueness due to a convex optimization problem and, in certain scenarios, may yield unproductive outcomes. These drawbacks are highlighted through a simple example. As an alternative, a novel approach called modal fusion is proposed. It tends towards favoring the estimate that is analytically closest to multiple local alternatives, even in cases of global aggregation where multiple modes exist.

The primary objective of this research is to examine host galaxies associated with Active Galactic Nuclei, or AGN. To compare different types of AGN, we created a relatively uniform dataset by applying uniform starlight corrections to near-infrared brightness and obtained average galaxy profiles, weighted by AGN luminosity. A sizeable majority of AGN, comprising LINERs, composite and starburst types, exhibit spiral or disk-like structures, regardless of inclination. In contrast, Type 1 and Type 2 Seyfert galaxies consistently show a central peak surrounded by a ring of emission, typically at an inclination of 60 degrees. This distinction sets them apart from other AGN, which have varying orientations. To explain the noticeable differences in galaxy morphology between Type 1 and Type 2 Seyfert galaxies, we propose a model involving a thinner, more uniform torus viewed edge-on in Type 1 galaxies, thereby concealing a visible host galaxy, as opposed to Type 2 galaxies with a thicker torus, allowing for a more direct host galaxy view.
